# Screenwriting Consultant

> Script notes, TV pilot notes, treatment analysis, logline punch-ups and career, deal and production advice from Matt Tabak, a former studio executive (Touchstone/Disney, Paramount, Warner Bros.), WGA screenwriter and director, attorney, and Professor of Screenwriting at Chapman University's Dodge College of Film and Media Arts. Based in Los Angeles; sessions by Zoom or phone.

## Key facts

- Developed the script that became Pretty Woman; bought and developed Face/Off; gave Se7en writer Andrew Kevin Walker his first screenwriting job.
- Developed 150+ projects and read 2,000+ scripts as a studio executive.
- Wrote and directed Auggie Rose (2000), his feature directorial debut, released on video as Beyond Suspicion. Wrote and produced The Other Zoey (2023).
- Writers Guild of America Award nominee (Adapted Long Form, The Stranger Beside Me, 2004); CableACE Award nominee (Dramatic Series, The Showtime 30-Minute Movie, 1995).
- Matt reads every page himself. No readers, no assistants, no AI. Coverage and notes are given verbally on a live Zoom or phone call; no written reports.
- Rates: feature screenplay notes $600; TV pilot notes $400; treatment analysis $350; logline punch-up $175; career, deal and production advice $200 an hour.

## Pages

- [Home and services](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/): services, rates, how it works, FAQ
- [About Matt Tabak](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/about/): career, credits and background
- [Blog](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/): screenwriting craft and business from a former studio executive
- [Resources](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/resources/): curated free screenwriting resources: where to read produced scripts and TV bibles, fellowships and labs, trusted contests, WGA resources, communities and free software
- [Script coverage](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/script-coverage/): what coverage is, pass/consider/recommend, and why Matt gives coverage verbally on a live call
- [How to write a logline](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-write-a-logline/): the four parts, length, common mistakes
- [18 types of movie ideas, and the engine that drives each one](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/types-of-movie-ideas/): Fish out of water, the underdog, the con, the night that goes completely wrong: 18 proven engines, with examples.
- [The Art of Dramatic Writing: what Lajos Egri gets right about premise, and where he’s overrated](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/lajos-egri-art-of-dramatic-writing/): Egri’s three-part premise, why the ending is already in it, where his method breaks down, and the one-sentence test worth stealing.
- [How to write a movie outline before you write page one](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-outline-a-screenplay/): Five outlining methods, how much detail you actually need, and how to stress-test your story before you write a single scene.
- [How to pitch a screenplay: lessons from the buyer's chair](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-pitch-a-screenplay/): How to structure a pitch, how long it should run, how to query, and how to make it easy for an executive to repeat to their boss.
- [How to pitch or submit a script to Netflix (and what really happens)](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-pitch-a-script-to-netflix/): Netflix's official policy on unsolicited scripts, why it exists, and the realistic routes a project takes to a Netflix executive.
- [How to take script notes without losing your voice](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-take-script-notes/): How to hear the note behind the note, triage feedback and rewrite without sanding off your voice.
- [How to write a film treatment that gets read](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-write-a-film-treatment/): What a treatment is, how long it should be, how to write one for a feature or a TV series, and the mistakes that get them put down.
- [How to write a TV pilot that makes a reader want episode 2](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/how-to-write-a-tv-pilot/): What a pilot must prove, premise vs. non-premise pilots, page counts, act breaks, bibles, and how pilots work as staffing samples.
- [Screenplay coverage example: what a studio reader's report looks like](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/script-coverage-example/): A full sample coverage report for an invented screenplay, annotated section by section by a former studio executive.
- [Three-act structure examples: how Pretty Woman, Face/Off and other hits break down](https://screenwritingconsultant.com/blog/three-act-structure-examples/): Pretty Woman, Face/Off, Die Hard and Get Out, broken down beat by beat, and how to use structure to diagnose your own draft.
